To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have developed a novel, engineered, and safe simulant that can serve as a replacement for MS2 in the testing, evaluation, and training of BW detection systems, and that the simulant is a DNA virus with the same size and morphology as the most dangerous BW threat agents.
we have developed a set of simulants for viruses in general, and for the family Poxviridae in particular.
we have successfully produced a virus-like particle that is a simulant for orthopoxviruse.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a simulant that more closely mimics the threat viruses of eukeryotes, particularly those in the poxvirus family.
developing a new, engineered, non-infectious, DNA virus simulant that is similar in size and structure to the orthopoxvirus family of agents.
the production of a virus that is similar to MS2 in many respects, but that also shares the size and genome structure of a virus of concern.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MS2 is a poor surrogate for the vast majority of viruses of concern.
MS2 is a good surrogate for the detection of RNA viruses in general, but is a poor surrogate for the detection and characterization of poxviruses.
the current state of the science of simulant development for viral threat agents is not sufficient to allow for realistic and reproducible testing and training.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have created a new simulant for use in biological defense testing, training and research that more closely mimics the threat agent of concern, the smallpox virus, than the current simulant.
we have successfully engineered a new simulant, a doublestranded, linear, DNA virus, that is similar to a viral threat agent in nearly every respect.

we have successfully produced a DNA virus that is similar in size, structure and composition to orthopoxviruse, and we have successfully produced the virus in both a wild-type and a genetically engineered form.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of MS2 as a surrogate for poxviruses is not appropriate.
we can use a combination of molecular biology, virology, biochemistry and structural biology techniques to create a new family of engineered simulants.
we have successfully developed a simulant that is a better surrogate for the orthopox family of virus than MS2.
